title: Wings rehearse in Nashville | 1974
content:
Wings rehearsed in Nashville, Tennessee, on 9 July 1974.

The rehearsals took place at the farm owned by songwriter Claude ‘Curly’ Putman Jr. Wings stayed at the farm, which they rented for $2,000 a week, and rehearsed in the garage.

They had been steadily adding songs to their repertoire since rehearsals began on 10 June. On this day they ran through all their songs performed so far, which included ‘Band On The Run’, ‘Bluebird’, ‘Go Now’, ‘Hi, Hi, Hi’, ‘Jet’, ‘Junior’s Farm’, ‘Let Me Roll It’, ‘Live And Let Die’, ‘Medicine Jar’, ‘Sally G’, and ‘Wild Life’.

Towards the end of the rehearsal they began working on Denny Laine’s song ‘Send Me The Heart’.

A meeting was also held with Brian Bolly, MPL’s managing director. He brought contracts for the non-McCartney members of Wings, offering them royalties on studio releases and a percentage of the takings from concert ticket sales.

This brought some security that was previously missing from the band, but Denny Laine demurred, saying it would make him an employee of Paul McCartney, and put him on an equal footing with newcomers Jimmy McCulloch and Geoff Britton. The contracts remained unsigned and were later scrapped.

The idea was really designed to make the other two guys feel more secure, but first of all, I decided I didn’t want to sign it because I’d never been on that kind of relationship with Paul anyway. Then it seemed like there was no point in having Wings on the basis of ‘You’re in the band sign here’.

We’ve got to have that fluid thing. Like, in the studio, we might want to bring in other musicians, and maybe the other two guys won’t be on every track.

Also with the three of us having been together for such a long time you can’t expect the other two to be so established. They’ve got to grow into it just like we’ve had to.

For myself, it’s better because I’m treated more like an equal – which I wouldn’t have been if I’d signed a contract. I didn’t want to sign, so I had a chat with Paul and found he didn’t want to bother with it either.

Denny Laine
New Musical Express, 17 August 1974
